{{Short description|Canadian chemist}}
{{More citations needed|date=May 2024}}

'''Rockcliffe St. J. Manley''' (26 March 1925 – 31 December 2011) was a Jamaican-Canadian chemist known for his development of the [[electrospinning]] technique of producing polymer nanofibres and for his work on [[cellulose]].

== Early life ==
Manley was born in [[Kingston, Jamaica|Kingston]], [[Jamaica]]. His parents were Harvey Arnold Manley and Vinette Madaline Bingham, and he had 3 brothers and one sister.

== Academic career ==
He spent most of his later academic career at [[McGill University]] in Canada, in the Pulp and Paper Science Division of the Chemistry Department.

In 1953 he received his PhD from McGill University on the subject “Rotations, Collisions and Orientations in Model Suspensions” (supervised by Stan Mason<ref>{{Cite web |title=Canadian Society of Rheology |url=https://www.polymtl.ca/scr-csr/en/stanley_mason.php |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=www.polymtl.ca}}</ref>), and published early papers on the physics of particle motions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Manley |first=Rockliffe St J. |others=S. (Supervisor) Mason |title=Rotations, collisions and orientations in model suspensions. |url=https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/concern/theses/dz010t91w |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=escholarship.mcgill.ca}}</ref>

He made substantial contributions to cellulose research, but he was the first person to publish the electrospinning of a [[polymer]] melt.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Larrondo |first1=L. |last2=St. John Manley |first2=R. |date=June 1981 |title=Electrostatic fiber spinning from polymer melts. I. Experimental observations on fiber formation and properties |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/pol.1981.180190601 |journal=Journal of Polymer Science: Polymer Physics Edition |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=909–920 |doi=10.1002/pol.1981.180190601|bibcode=1981JPoSB..19..909L |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Manley electrospun molten polymers, and showed that they (if thin enough) had a shish-kebab structure.<ref name=":0" /> Later the technique of [[electrospinning]] was carried out by other authors using polymer solutions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=D. |last2=Xia |first2=Y. |date=2004-07-19 |title=Electrospinning of Nanofibers: Reinventing the Wheel? |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adma.200400719 |journal=Advanced Materials |language=en |volume=16 |issue=14 |pages=1151–1170 |doi=10.1002/adma.200400719 |bibcode=2004AdM....16.1151L |s2cid=137659394 |issn=0935-9648|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Manley's PhD student, Lidia Larrondo,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Larrondo |first=Lidia E. |others=Dr R. St John Manley |title=Electrostatic fiber spinning from polymer melts |url=https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/concern/theses/gb19f845r |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=escholarship.mcgill.ca}}</ref> with whom he published the electrospinning work, was a refugee from [[General Pinochet]]’s Chile.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bastow |first=Kathryn |date=2021-10-14 |title=Forgotten Histories of Black Engineers and Scientists |url=https://engineering.blogs.bristol.ac.uk/forgotten-histories-of-black-engineers-and-scientists/ |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=We are Engineering |language=en-GB}}</ref>

He developed a chain folding theory for the structure of cellulose,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Manley |first=R. St John |date=December 1964 |title=Fine Structure of Native Cellulose Microfibrils |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/2041155a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=204 |issue=4964 |pages=1155–1157 |doi=10.1038/2041155a0 |bibcode=1964Natur.204.1155M |s2cid=4153633 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which was criticised at the time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gillis |first1=P. P. |last2=Mark |first2=R. E. |last3=Tang |first3=R. -C. |date=1969-11-01 |title=Elastic stiffness of crystalline cellulose in the folded-chain solid state |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00555317 |journal=Journal of Materials Science |language=en |volume=4 |issue=11 |pages=1003–1007 |doi=10.1007/BF00555317 |bibcode=1969JMatS...4.1003G |s2cid=137347893 |issn=1573-4803|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He based his work on that of the [[University of Bristol|Bristol University]] physicist [[Andrew Keller]]. Keller had come up with a structure for polyethylene that required the polymer chains to fold, in what are now known as lamellae, making up a spherulitic structure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Keller |first=A. |date=1957-09-01 |title=A note on single crystals in polymers: Evidence for a folded chain configuration |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/14786435708242746 |journal=The Philosophical Magazine |volume=2 |issue=21 |pages=1171–1175 |doi=10.1080/14786435708242746 |bibcode=1957PMag....2.1171K |issn=0031-8086|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Manley applied the same theories to cellulose, carrying out high resolution [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]]. Later it was generally accepted that the crystalline structure of cellulose is not chain folded.

Manley won the [[Anselme Payen Award]] from the Cellulose and Renewable Materials Division of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 2002.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Anselme Payen Award |url=https://acscell.org/awards/the-anselme-payen-award/ |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=Cellulose and Renewable Materials |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==

* 2002 - [[Anselme Payen Award]] by the American Chemical Society
* 1976 - Fellow of the American Physical Society
* Fellow of the [[Chemical Institute of Canada]]

== Personal life and death ==
He was married twice, to Ulla-Brita Henriksson who predeceased him, and later to Linda St-Denis.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |title=Rockliffe MANLEY Obituary (2012) - Montreal, Quebec - The Gazette |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/legacyremembers/rockliffe-manley-obituary?id=44660518 |access-date=2026-06-21 |website=www.legacy.com |language=en}}</ref> His second cousin was the Prime Minister of Jamaica - [[Michael Norman Manley]]. He had one son, Peter Henrik Manley and four grand children. He was also step father to Martin & Annie St-Denis.<ref name="auto"/> Manley died on 31 December 2011 in [[St. Mary's Hospital (Montreal)]].<ref name="auto"/>
